analysis.one_liner: Charges the largest fossil fuel companies up to $1 trillion for past emissions to fund climate disaster recovery.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat without a hearing or vote since being referred to three House committees in February 2025, with 25 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a one-time $1 trillion assessment on the country's largest fossil fuel extractors and refiners, split among them according to each company's share of carbon dioxide emissions released from 2000 through 2023. The money would go into a new Polluters Pay Climate Fund for disaster recovery, resilient infrastructure, and climate adaptation, with 40 percent reserved for environmental justice communities. Companies could pay by September 30, 2026 or in nine annual installments.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by climate-driven disasters — floods, hurricanes, wildfires, extreme heat — would get a dedicated funding stream for recovery and resilience, including at least $15 billion a year for FEMA programs and $6 billion a year for Clean Air Act climate grants. Forty percent of annual fund spending would be reserved for environmental justice communities: communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities that bear disproportionate climate and pollution burdens. Taxpayers generally benefit because disaster costs the industry would help cover now come out of federal budgets.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a one-time $1 trillion assessment, apportioned among fossil fuel companies in proportion to each company's share of covered carbon dioxide emissions above 1 billion metric tons during 2000-2023.

Creates a Polluters Pay Climate Fund dedicated to disaster recovery, climate-resilient infrastructure, adaptation planning, and related investments, with a 40 percent annual set-aside for environmental justice communities.

Directs at least $15 billion per year to FEMA disaster response and resilience programs (including $3 billion for the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program) and at least $6 billion per year to climate grants under the Clean Air Act.
Lets companies pay either in full by September 30, 2026 or in nine annual installments, with the balance accelerated if a company sells off assets or shuts down.
Preserves state lawsuits and other remedies against fossil fuel companies, and prohibits the assessment from being used as evidence or to offset damages in those cases.
Bars companies from deducting the assessment as a business expense on their federal taxes.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that extracted fossil fuels or refined crude oil in the United States and are responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions between 2000 and 2023 — the largest oil, gas, and coal producers and refiners — would owe the assessment, with joint liability across parent companies and successors. Some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers through fuel and energy prices, though as a one-time levy on past operations rather than a recurring per-unit fee, the pass-through would be limited by competition and by how much of the bill falls on production that has already ended.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major fossil fuel extraction and refining companies

drawbacks.text: Because the assessment reaches back to emissions from 2000 through 2023, affected companies would almost certainly challenge it as a retroactive levy, and litigation could delay or prevent collections.
The fund's money is only available as provided in annual appropriations acts, so the trillion-dollar authorization would still depend on Congress actually appropriating it year by year.
Fossil fuel companies could pass part of the assessment to consumers through higher fuel prices, since the tax falls on companies whose products are household energy essentials.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential public benefit is large: a dedicated trillion-dollar stream for disaster recovery and resilience at a time when climate disasters cost the country roughly $150 billion a year, much of it borne by taxpayers. The main costs are the risk that companies pass part of the tab to consumers and the likelihood of years of litigation over the retroactive structure. A further design weakness is that the fund depends on annual appropriations, so the headline number is not money in hand. On balance, the bill's benefits to the public outweigh its drawbacks if it works as written, but the retroactive structure and the appropriations dependency make the outcome less certain than the topline suggests.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to three House committees the day it was introduced and has sat there ever since, with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 7, 2025 and referred the same day to the Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce committees, with no lead committee designated.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears anywhere in the bill's action history.
The bill's 25 cosponsors are all House Democrats; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies are better off so far: no assessment has been collected and none appears close to a vote. Federal, state, and local budgets continue to absorb the cost of climate disasters that the bill would have shifted to the industry, and communities waiting on resilience funding keep waiting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies that avoided the fee

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the primary committee of jurisdiction
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral.

against.name: Speaker Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to three committees without designating a lead panel, and never brought it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 initial supporters are House Democrats — 25 of 217 in the caucus — and no Republican has cosponsored, while the Republican House leadership has not advanced the bill.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel extraction and refining companies
industries.note: The companies responsible for the most emissions since 2000 would owe shares of a $1 trillion assessment, with joint liability across corporate groups and no tax deduction. Because their products are household energy essentials, part of the cost could surface in fuel prices, but the bill also keeps state lawsuits against them fully intact.

Fund spending on resilient infrastructure, grid upgrades, water systems, and FEMA-backed projects would create demand for construction and engineering work. Those gains track the public's interest in better flood and wildfire protection.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since February 2025, support drawn entirely from House Democrats, and Republicans controlling the chamber and its committee calendar, the bill is unlikely to reach the floor this Congress. The most likely path is that it sits until the Congress ends in January 2027, though supporters could reintroduce it in the next Congress.
